analysis.one_liner: Phased out federal sugar price supports and marketing quotas that keep U.S. sugar prices high.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 64 cosponsors to phase out the federal sugar program died in the House Agriculture Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law props up sugar prices through government loans to sugar processors and import quotas, and U.S. sugar prices have long run well above the world price. This bill would have gradually cut the government's sugar loan rates from 2001 through 2004, converted the loans to a type that does not guarantee growers a price floor, repealed the sugar marketing quota system, and ended all federal sugar price support after the 2004 crop. It also directed the President to make sure adequate sugar supplies reach the U.S. market at prices no higher than the world price or the loan rate. The practical effect would have been lower sugar prices for households and for food companies that use sugar.
analysis.who_benefits: American households that buy sugar and food companies that use it as an ingredient — candy makers, bakers, cereal and beverage producers — would have gained from sugar prices drifting down toward world levels. Taxpayers would also have been protected from losses when sugar processors forfeited government-backed loans, as happened in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts the raw cane sugar loan rate from 18 cents per pound to 14 cents by the 2004 crop, stepping down each year, which lowers the government-guaranteed price floor under the sugar market.
It ends all federal price support — loans, payments, or purchases — for sugarcane and sugar beet crops from 2005 onward, leaving the sugar market to set prices.
It repeals the sugar and crystalline fructose marketing quota and allotment system, the domestic production limits that restrict who can grow and process sugar.
It converts nonrecourse loans, which let processors hand sugar to the government instead of repaying when prices fall, into recourse loans that must be repaid, shielding taxpayers from forfeitures.
It directs the President to use all available authority to ensure adequate raw sugar supplies reach the U.S. market at no more than the higher of the world price or the loan rate.

analysis.who_pays: Sugar cane growers and processors, concentrated in Florida, Louisiana, Texas and Hawaii, and sugar beet growers and processors in the Midwest and northern plains, would lose the price supports and production quotas that keep their returns well above what an open market would pay. Rural communities built around beet sugar processing would feel the squeeze.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sugar cane and beet growers and processors

drawbacks.text: Ending price supports and quotas would reduce the incomes of cane and beet growers and processors, and the towns and workforces tied to sugar processing would bear real costs during the transition.

Supporters of the existing program argue that when world prices fall below the cost of production — as they often have, in part because other countries subsidize their own growers — removing the U.S. floor could shrink domestic supply and leave the country dependent on imported sugar. The bill's four-year phase-down and its directive to keep supplies flowing at the loan rate were the response to that concern, but the risk to growers was real.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are broad but small per person: the sugar program keeps retail sugar prices well above world levels, and every household pays a little more at the grocery store, while the benefits of the program flow to a few thousand grower-processor operations. The bill phased the change in over four years, which softened the blow to growers, but the objection that domestic growers could be squeezed by subsidized foreign competition is serious and was the program's core rationale. On balance, the cost of the program falls on millions of consumers to benefit a small, concentrated group — which is why the bill's repeal approach weighs in favor of passage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Specialty Crops subcommittee in June 2001, and it sat there without a hearing or vote until that Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Miller of Florida introduced the Sugar Program Reform Act on June 6, 2001, with 50 original cosponsors from both parties.
It was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture on June 6, 2001.
On June 13, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Specialty Crops and Foreign Agriculture Programs, where no further action was taken.
The bill ended the Congress with 64 cosponsors, 37 Republicans and 27 Democrats, but never received a markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar growers and processors came out ahead: the program that keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels stayed intact, and consumers and sugar-using food companies continued to pay the difference. No alternatives were enacted in this Congress either.

for.name: Rep. Dan Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sugar Program Reform Act to phase out sugar price supports and quotas.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee (Chair Larry Combest)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the sugar program
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or hearing; the bill died there.

against.name: Sugar industry (cane and beet growers and processors)
against.role: Industry protected by the sugar program
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts to phase out the sugar program and defended the existing price support and quota system during the 2001 farm bill debate.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — the original 50 cosponsors split 27 Democrats and 23 Republicans, and the bill finished with 37 Republican and 27 Democratic cosponsors; the bill died from committee inaction rather than a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Sugarcane growers and processors (Florida, Louisiana, Texas, Hawaii)
industries.note: The bill would have phased out the loan-rate floor and ended price support after the 2004 crop, cutting the guaranteed prices that keep cane sugar returns above open-market levels. Consumers effectively pay the program's cost through higher sugar prices.

industries.industry: Sugar beet growers and processors (Upper Midwest, northern plains)
industries.note: The bill cut the beet sugar loan rate on the same schedule and ended all beet sugar price support from 2005 onward, and repealed the quota system that allocates who may grow and process sugar beets.

industries.industry: Sugar-using food manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals, beverages)
industries.note: Sugar is a major input cost, and the U.S. program keeps domestic prices well above world levels; a market-clearing price would lower their costs and, in principle, consumer prices. These companies supported reform through the Coalition for Sugar Reform during this period.

industries.industry: Corn sweetener producers (high-fructose corn syrup and crystalline fructose)
industries.note: The bill repeals the crystalline fructose marketing quota provisions, opening that market to corn refiners, and cheaper sugar would compete more directly with corn sweeteners.
